name: Hussites
info: The Hussites were a Czech proto-Protestant movement that followed the teachings of Jan Hus after his execution in 1415, fought the Hussite Wars of 1420 to 1434, and left a tradition that continues in several churches today.

facts.where: the Kingdom of Bohemia and the other Lands of the Bohemian Crown, including Moravia and Silesia; inroads into the north of the Kingdom of Hungary (now Slovakia); small temporary communities in Poland-Lithuania and Transylvania; later refuge communities in Lissa (Leszno), the Low Countries and Herrnhut in Saxony
facts.period: organised 1415–1419; Four Articles of Prague 1420; Hussite Wars 1420–1434; Compactata of Prague 1433; Battle of Lipany 1434; religious peace of Kutná Hora 1485; Catholicism reimposed after White Mountain 1620; Herrnhut settlement 1722; Czechoslovak Hussite Church after 1918
facts.figures: Jan Hus, the reformer executed in 1415; Jan Žižka, Taborite leader who resisted five crusades; Jacob of Mies, author of the Four Articles; Jerome of Prague, a major theologian; Petr Chelčický, pacifist whose teachings underlay the Unitas Fratrum; Jan Amos Comenius, who fled to the Low Countries
facts.outcome: the moderate Utraquists became the dominant Hussite group in Bohemia and the Taborites were defeated in 1434; Catholics and Utraquists had legal equality from 1485; Catholicism was reimposed after 1620; the tradition continues in the Moravian Church, the Unity of the Brethren and the Czechoslovak Hussite Church

t: The Hussites followed the reformer Jan Hus, burned at the stake at the Council of Constance on 6 July 1415, and took the chalice of wine given to the laity as their emblem.

They were not one movement but several parties: moderate Utraquists, who wished to leave the order of the Church untouched, and radical Taborites, Orebites and Orphans, who held to Wycliffe’s teaching and wished to remove the hierarchy.

After the crusades and civil wars of the Hussite Wars (1420–1434) the Utraquists came out dominant, Catholics and Utraquists were given legal equality in 1485, and Roman Catholicism was reimposed in Bohemia only after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620.
dyk: The name Tábor was a play on words: in Czech it meant a camp or encampment, and it was also the traditional name of the mountain on which Jesus was expected to return.
ev: Jan Hus is tried for heresy by the Council of Constance and burned at the stake
News of the death of King Wenceslaus produces a revolution in Prague: churches and monasteries are destroyed and church property seized
The Four Articles of Prague, written by Jacob of Mies, set out the programme of the moderate Hussites
A Bohemian–Moravian assembly in Prague accepts the Compactata, granting communion in both kinds
The Calixtines and Catholics together destroy the Taborites at the Battle of Lipany
The Diet of Kutná Hora makes an agreement between Catholics and Utraquists
The Battle of White Mountain opens the way for the reimposition of Roman Catholicism
A settlement of Hussites at Herrnhut in Saxony leads to the emergence of the Moravian Church

sections.background:
In the 9th century the Byzantine Greek missionaries Saints Cyril and Methodius introduced the Byzantine Rite, in the Old Church Slavonic liturgical language, into the Czech lands, together with communion under both kinds given to the laity. A few decades later German-speaking bishops from East Francia, beginning with Wiching, imposed the Latin Roman Rite, in which only the clergy receive communion under both kinds. The Czechs of that time could understand the Slavonic liturgy but not the Latin one. Wiching obtained a papal bull from Pope Stephen V, Quia te zelo fidei, banning the Slavonic liturgy in the Roman church. For this reason there was neither a Czech liturgy nor communion under both kinds when Jan Hus proposed those reforms in the 14th century.

Hus was arrested in 1414, and the authorities of Bohemia and Moravia appealed urgently and repeatedly to King Sigismund to release him. The Council of Constance tried him for heresy and put him to death at the stake on 6 July 1415. When the news arrived, disturbances broke out, directed primarily against the clergy and especially the monks; even the Archbishop narrowly escaped. The treatment of Hus was felt to be a disgrace to the whole country, and his death was seen as a criminal act. Hussitism organised itself in the years 1415 to 1419, influenced by the teachings of John Wycliffe.
sections.aims:
The Hussites were never a unitary movement. They formed two parties from the beginning, with a smaller number withdrawing from both around the pacifist Petr Chelčický, whose teachings would form the foundation of the Unitas Fratrum. The moderate party, the Utraquists or Calixtines, followed Hus more closely and sought reform while leaving the whole hierarchical and liturgical order of the Church untouched. Their programme was the Four Articles of Prague, written by Jacob of Mies and agreed in July 1420 in Latin, Czech and German: free preaching of the Word of God throughout Bohemia and Moravia; communion under both kinds, bread and wine, for the laity; the removal of secular power from the clergy; and secular punishment for mortal sins among clergy and laity alike. The names come from the Latin calix, chalice, and utraque, both, since the party stressed the second article.

The radical parties, the Taborites, Orebites and Orphans, identified more boldly with Wycliffe, sharing his hatred of the monastic clergy and his wish to return the Church to its supposed condition in the time of the apostles. That meant removing the hierarchy and secularising church property. They denied transubstantiation, the principal point separating them from the Utraquists, and preached the sufficientia legis Christi: the Bible as the sole rule for society, in political and civil matters as well as in the church. As early as 1416 they rejected what they believed had no basis in the Bible, among it the veneration of saints and images, fasts, the oath and indulgences, and they chose their own priests.
sections.events:
A league of lords pledged to protect free preaching on their estates, and in 1417 several lesser nobles and some barons removed Catholic priests from their parishes and installed priests willing to give communion in both wine and bread. The chalice became the central symbol of the movement. King Wenceslaus IV refused to join the league and approached a newly formed Roman Catholic League of lords. In 1418 Sigismund won his brother over to the council’s side, Hussite statesmen and army leaders had to leave the country and Catholic priests were reinstated. Wenceslaus died of a stroke in 1419, and a revolution swept the country: churches and monasteries were destroyed and the Hussite nobility seized church property. Sigismund could take his kingdom only by force, and Pope Martin V declared a crusade.

The radicals’ first armed assault fell on Ústí on the river Lužnice. As it could not be defended, they settled on a nearby hill and founded the town of Tábor. The Hussites campaigned defensively at first, and from 1427 they assumed the offensive, crossing the borders into neighbouring countries. Jan Žižka led a fierce resistance to five consecutive crusades. On 23 March 1430 Joan of Arc dictated a letter threatening to lead a crusading army against them, but she was captured two months later. The Hussites were invited to the Council of Basel on 15 October 1431, and discussions began on 10 January 1432 without agreement.
sections.people:
Jan Hus (born 1368, executed 1415) was the reformer whose teachings gave the movement its name. The English reformer John Wycliffe influenced the Hussites, and Petr Chelčický and Jerome of Prague were major Hussite theologians. Jacob of Mies wrote the Four Articles of Prague. Several Hussites became Czech national heroes, among them the Taborite leader Jan Žižka, who led a fierce resistance to the crusades proclaimed on Hussite Bohemia by the papacy.

Besides the Utraquist majority and the Taborites it lists the Adamites, the Orebites and the Orphans. The moderates include the Prague Hussites, the Bohemian Hussite nobility, and the Hussites of Žatec and Louny. The Orebites, later called Orphans, were an eastern Bohemian sect based in Hradec Králové and usually supported the Taborites. On the other side stood King Wenceslaus IV, who at first gave free vent to his indignation at the course of events in Constance, and his brother Sigismund. Pope Martin V had attacked Hus with relentless severity as Cardinal Otto of Colonna and wished to eradicate his doctrine completely. Jan Amos Comenius was among those who fled to western Europe, mainly the Low Countries, after 1620.
sections.outcomes:
The Compactata of Prague, accepted on 30 November 1433, granted communion in both kinds to all who desired it, on the understanding that Christ was entirely present in each kind and on the condition that the rest of the Hussite reforms would no longer be emphasised. Free preaching was granted only conditionally, since the Church hierarchy had to approve priests, and the Prague demand against the secular power of the clergy was almost reversed. The Taborites refused to conform. The Calixtines united with the Roman Catholics and destroyed them at the Battle of Lipany on 30 May 1434. The Hussite movement continued in Poland for five more years, until Polish royal forces defeated the Polish Hussites at Grotniki. The assembly of Jihlava in 1436 confirmed the Compactata, and Sigismund obtained the Bohemian crown. In 1444 the assembly in Prague rejected Wyclif’s doctrine of the Lord’s Supper as heresy. Most Taborites went over to the Utraquists, and the rest joined the Brothers of the Law of Christ.

In 1462 Pope Pius II declared the Compacta void and prohibited communion in both kinds. King George of Podebrady refused to promise harmony with Rome, which led to the Bohemian–Hungarian War of 1468 to 1478. The Diet of Kutná Hora in 1485 produced an agreement that lasted thirty-one years, and the Diet of 1512 permanently established equal rights. In the north of Hungary the movement was rejected and gained infamy for the plundering of Hussite soldiers. It remained a regional movement that failed to expand farther.
sections.legacy:
Hussites are described as one of the most important forerunners of the Protestant Reformation. A predominantly religious movement, it was propelled by social issues and strengthened Czech national awareness. When Martin Luther appeared the Utraquist clergy hailed him, and Luther was astonished to find so many points of agreement between the doctrines of Hus and his own. Not all Utraquists approved of the German Reformation; a schism arose, and some returned to the Roman doctrine, while others had organised the Unitas Fratrum as early as 1457. Under Emperor Maximilian II the Bohemian assembly established the Confessio Bohemica, on which Lutherans, Reformed and Bohemian Brethren agreed, and from then on Hussitism began to die out.

After the Battle of White Mountain on 8 November 1620 Catholicism was re-established with vigour. Leaders and members of the Unitas Fratrum had to leave or practise their beliefs secretly, and the largest remaining communities were at Lissa (Leszno) in Poland and in small groups in Moravia. A settlement of Hussites at Herrnhut in Saxony in 1722 caused the emergence of the Moravian Church. In 1918 the Czech lands regained independence as Czechoslovakia, and the Hussite tradition is linked to Masaryk and to the name of the Czechoslovak legions. Today the tradition is represented in the Moravian Church, the Unity of the Brethren and the Czechoslovak Hussite Church.

summary: The Hussites were a Czech proto-Protestant movement that followed Jan Hus after his execution in 1415 and fought the Hussite Wars of 1420 to 1434. The moderate Utraquists prevailed over the radical Taborites, and the tradition continues in the Moravian Church and the Czechoslovak Hussite Church.

The article gives Hus as 'b. 1368–1415, fl. 1401–1415' (garbled); I wrote born 1368, executed 1415.
Left out: the Joan of Arc letter's detail beyond one sentence; the Hussite Bible and see-also items; the claim that the Council 'lured' Hus with a letter of indemnity (loaded wording, one source).
The article's sentence that the Hussite movement in Poland continued 'another five years' until Grotniki is kept; its date (1439) is not given.
